newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe resigns after left-wing victory.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe resigns after left-wing victory.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe resigned on Monday and after a stunning Socialist-led election win heralded a new European Union policy for France, less focused on austerity to qualify for a single currency.

The French stock market fell 2.76 percent at the opening while the franc and French bonds also came under pressure. Final results showed the Socialists would need support from the Communists, who oppose deeper European integration.

Humiliated by the defeat, conservative Juppe tendered his resignation to his long-time mentor President Jacques Chirac, paving the way to the appointment of Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin as prime minister.

Chirac, who beat Jospin to the presidency in 1995, summoned him to the Elysee Palace at 11.30 a.m. (0930 GMT). The president was expected to ask him to form a government, opening an awkward period of power-sharing between ideological rivals.

Final results showed the Socialists and their allies won 273 seats in the 577-seat National Assembly and the Communists 38 after Sunday's decisive runoff round. The ecologists won seven, their first seats in parliament.

The outgoing centre-right coalition, which had held 464 seats in the outgoing Assembly, crashed to 257. The far-right National Front won one and an independent in the French Caribbean island of Martinique won one seat.

Triumphantly elected only two years ago, Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on April 21 and called a snap election in hopes of ensuring himself a friendly majority for the rest of his seven-year term until 2002.
He said France needed a "new elan" to prepare for a single European currency from 1999, but his pleas fell flat in a country more worried by his broken promises on job creation and lower taxes.
Jospin said after his victory on Sunday that the people had voted for a change of direction in European policy, but he did not call into question the planned single European currency.
Party spokesman Francois Hollande reaffirmed the Socialists' pledge that they would not impose further austerity to qualify for the euro and reiterated four conditions for joining.
"We all stand to gain if...Europe no longer means austerity," he said in a radio interview.

Hollande reaffirmed the Socialist conditions for the euro -- entry of Italy and Spain from the start, creation of a political counterweight to offset the power of a European central bank, creation of an EU pact of solidarity and growth to boost jobs, and that the euro should not be overvalued.

The Communists started to flex their muscles on Monday, saying they would disclose a list of demands, including relaxing the criteria for a single currency, to their Socialist allies as the price of joining a government.
Pierre Zarka, a member of the Communist Party leadership, said the conditions, drawn from a joint pre-election declaration, also included wage rises and cuts in working hours.
"We have put precise questions and we expect answers," Zarka told France Inter radio.
Socialist policies are also perceived by markets as less favourable to the corporate sector. The party wants to halt privatisations of companies like France Telecom or Air France.

The Socialists have pledged to create 700,000 jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector, over the next three years, and reduce the working week from 39 hours to 35 over five years without loss of pay.

Figures published on Monday showed that unemployment fell in April for the third month in a row, dipping 6,400 or 0.2 percent to 3,081,100. But the jobless rate was unchanged at a record 12.8 percent.
French media stressed the vote was a rebuke to Chirac by giving a new chance to the Socialists just four years after a right-wing landslide.
Writer Jean d'Ormesson, of the French Academy, said in Le Figaro that "the French tried the right. And then the left. And then the right again. And then the left again."
"They are like poor birds banging their heads against a window, like brainless sheep vainly seeking an exit. Once again, I doubt that they have knocked at the right door," he said.
